2025-1.why: A monetary union is a group of countries that share one currency and one monetary policy, as the euro area does.

not.B: A free trade area removes trade barriers between members; each keeps its own currency.
not.C: A bilateral trade agreement is about trade between two countries, not their currency.
not.D: A multilateral trade agreement involves three or more countries and is about trade, not a shared currency.

2025-2.why: Cheaper energy lowers the cost of transport and production, which makes trading goods across borders cheaper and speeds up integration.

not.A: Less labour mobility means fewer workers moving between countries, which slows globalisation.
not.B: Dearer communication makes it harder to trade and invest across borders.
not.D: Higher tariffs are protection: they reduce trade.

2025-3.why: X is the education indicator for a developing economy (low literacy) and Y is the health indicator for an advanced economy (high life expectancy).

not.A: Low literacy fits X, but an advanced economy has high, not low, life expectancy.
not.B: High life expectancy fits Y, but a developing economy has low literacy.
not.C: Both are the wrong way around.

2025-4.why: In a downturn households spend less, so revenue from taxes on spending such as the GST falls automatically.

not.A: Interest rates are set by the Reserve Bank and are not a component of the budget outcome.
not.C: Unemployment benefit payments rise in a downturn as more people lose work.
not.D: Lower revenue and higher welfare spending push the budget towards deficit, so borrowing rises.

2025-5.why: A private good is excludable and rival. A fare excludes people who do not pay, and a seat taken by one passenger cannot be used by another.

not.A: Public transport is excludable: you need a ticket. Being funded from tax does not decide the type of good.
not.C: It is rival, but it is excludable by price, not non-excludable.
not.D: Who provides a good does not decide whether it is public or private; excludability and rivalry do.

2025-6.why: Macroeconomic policy (fiscal and monetary) works on aggregate demand to smooth the business cycle.

not.A: Productivity and efficiency are the aim of microeconomic policy.
not.B: Shifting aggregate supply is the rationale for microeconomic policy.
not.D: Environmental sustainability is pursued through environmental policies, and it is not the main rationale for macroeconomic policy.

2025-7.why: The multiplier is 50 ÷ 10 = 5. Since k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC), 1 − MPC = 0.2, so MPC = 0.8.

not.A: 0.2 is the MPS (1 ÷ 5), not the MPC.
not.B: An MPC of 0.4 gives a multiplier of about 1.7, not 5.
not.C: An MPC of 0.5 gives a multiplier of 2, not 5.

2025-8.why: A regional business cycle is the pattern of economic activity shared by neighbouring countries whose economies are closely linked by trade and investment.

not.A: Regional here means a region of the world, not rural areas within a country.
not.B: It describes fluctuations, not stability, and a region rather than the whole globe.
not.C: It is about a group of countries, not the states inside one economy.

2025-9.why: Injections are I + G + X = 20 + 80 + 60 = 160. Leakages are S + T + M = 10 + 70 + 50 = 130. Injections are greater.

not.A: Exports (60) are greater than imports (50), so there is a trade surplus.
not.B: Government spending (80) is greater than taxation (70), so the budget is in deficit.
not.D: Leakages (130) are less than injections (160).

2025-10.why: Aid with no conditions attached is a transfer with nothing received in return, recorded in secondary income on the current account. Money leaving Australia is a debit.

not.A: The money is leaving Australia, so it is a debit, not a credit.
not.C: Only conditional (capital) aid goes in the capital account, and an outflow is not a credit.
not.D: It is a debit, but unconditional aid belongs in the current account. The capital account records conditional aid for capital projects.

2025-11.why: Automatic stabilisers (progressive income tax and unemployment benefits) change with the business cycle without any new decision, so they move the cyclical component.

not.B: External is not a component of the budget outcome.
not.C: The structural component reflects deliberate policy, with the effect of the cycle removed.
not.D: Discretionary changes are deliberate decisions by the government, the opposite of automatic.

2025-12.why: An emissions trading scheme puts a price on pollution and lets firms buy and sell permits, so the market decides where emissions are cut.

not.B: A tax on electric and hybrid cars would discourage cleaner cars and make outcomes worse.
not.C: Closing power stations is direct regulation, not the use of market forces.
not.D: Fines are a penalty set by regulation; they are not a market in which prices are set by trading.

2025-13.why: Current account = (150 − 130) + (60 − 50) − 50 + 10 = −10. With a floating rate the current account and the capital and financial account sum to zero, so capital and financial must be +10. With a capital account of 70, the financial account is 10 − 70 = −60.

not.A: −80 comes from treating the current account as +10: the two sides must offset, not match.
not.C: $10 billion is the whole capital and financial account, before taking out the capital account of 70.
not.D: $280 billion comes from adding items together rather than balancing the accounts.

2025-14.why: Headline inflation rose (4.5% to 5%) while underlying fell (3.8% to 3.4%). A drought raises food prices, a volatile item that affects headline but is removed from underlying. Lower freight costs reduce prices across the economy, lowering underlying inflation.

not.B: Higher tariffs and a higher minimum wage raise costs broadly, so underlying inflation would rise, not fall.
not.C: Microeconomic reform lowers costs, so it does not explain higher headline inflation, and an oil conflict would not lower underlying inflation.
not.D: A fuel excise discount lowers fuel prices, which would reduce headline inflation.

2025-15.why: Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ CPI × 100. Year 1: 18 ÷ 90 × 100 = 20. Year 2: 22 ÷ 110 × 100 = 20. Real GDP did not change, so growth is 0%.

not.B: 4 is the rise in nominal GDP in dollars ($22b − $18b), not a growth rate.
not.C: 20 is the level of real GDP in both years, not its growth.
not.D: 22% is the growth in nominal GDP (and in prices). Once inflation is removed nothing is left.

2025-16.why: Net foreign liabilities = what the country owes the world minus what the world owes it. Liabilities: 3.0 + 1.8 = 4.8. Assets: 1.2 + 0.5 = 1.7. 4.8 − 1.7 = $3.1 million.

not.A: $6.5 million adds all four items together instead of subtracting assets.
not.B: $4.8 million is the liabilities only; foreign assets have not been subtracted.
not.D: $500 000 is just one line of the table.

2025-17.why: A smaller quota lets in fewer imports, so supply falls and the price rises above X. Because the quota still exists, the price stays below P1, the price with no imports at all. P2 is the only price between X and P1.

not.A: P1 is the price with no imports at all. The quota is reduced, not eliminated in favour of a total ban.
not.C: P3 is below X. A tighter quota raises the price; it does not lower it.
not.D: P4 is the world price, which applies only with no quota at all.

2025-18.why: Before the tariff the price is $20: demand 600, domestic supply 200, imports 400, so foreign revenue is 400 × $20 = $8000. With the tariff the price is $30: demand 500, domestic supply 300, imports 200. Foreign producers still receive only the world price, so revenue is 200 × $20 = $4000. The fall is $4000.

not.A: $2000 is the tariff revenue collected by the government (200 × $10).
not.C: $8000 is foreign producers' revenue before the tariff, not the decrease.
not.D: $16 000 is too large: total import spending was only $8000 to begin with.

2025-19.why: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Year 1: 110 × 100 ÷ 100 = 110. Year 2: 90 × 110 ÷ 100 = 99.

not.A: 90 and 110 are read straight off the table (the Year 2 terms of trade and import price index), not calculated.
not.B: 99 is the Year 2 export price index, not Year 1.
not.C: 110 is right for Year 1, but 90 is the Year 2 terms of trade, not the export price index.

2025-20.why: The tax must equal the external cost: the vertical gap between the social cost and private cost curves. At Q3 that gap runs from P1 (private cost) up to P3 (social cost). The same gap can be seen at Q2, from P0 to P2.

not.A: P0 to P1 is only part of the gap between the curves.
not.B: P1 to P2 is the rise in the market price after the tax, which is smaller than the tax because producers bear part of it.
not.C: P2 to P3 is only part of the gap between the curves.

2024-1.why: The World Bank lends for development projects to reduce poverty and raise living standards in developing countries.

not.B: The WTO sets and enforces the rules of world trade.
not.C: The IMF looks after the stability of the international financial system and helps countries in financial crisis.
not.D: The OECD is a forum of mostly advanced economies that researches and coordinates policy.

2024-2.why: Centralised wage fixing sets minimum pay and conditions for everyone, which protects workers with little bargaining power.

not.A: Uniform wages make it harder for labour to move to growing industries, so structural change is slower.
not.B: Wage flexibility is a feature of decentralised bargaining, not a centralised system.
not.D: Centralised systems compress wage differences, and greater inequality would not be a benefit.

2024-3.why: In the short term, stronger demand lowers unemployment but pushes prices up, and slowing inflation costs jobs (the Phillips curve trade-off).

not.B: Economic growth creates jobs, so growth and low unemployment go together.
not.C: There is no direct short-term trade-off between these two.
not.D: Inflation is not an objective (price stability is), and it has no clear short-term conflict with sustainability.

2024-4.why: With open markets, foreign firms can sell goods below cost (dumping), which can drive efficient local firms out of business.

not.A: Greater competition is usually counted as an advantage: it lifts efficiency and lowers prices.
not.B: Free trade lowers domestic prices by letting in cheaper imports.
not.D: Access to bigger markets lets firms gain economies of scale, an advantage.

2024-5.why: A holding below 10% of a company is portfolio investment. Foreign money flowing into Australia is a credit on the financial account.

not.A: Direct investment needs 10% or more of the company, and an inflow is not a debit.
not.B: It is a credit, but 5% is too small to be direct investment.
not.C: It is portfolio investment, but money coming in is a credit, not a debit.

2024-6.why: Labour force = employed + unemployed = 7 + 2 = 9 million. Participation rate = 9 ÷ 11 (working age population) × 100 = 82%.

not.A: 44% is employed people as a share of the total population (7 ÷ 16).
not.B: 56% uses the total population (9 ÷ 16) instead of the working age population.
not.C: 78% is employed ÷ labour force (7 ÷ 9), the employment rate.

2024-7.why: Income rose by 100 (375 to 475) and savings rose by 40 (160 to 200), so MPS = 0.4 and MPC = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6.

not.A: 0.34 does not come from the changes in income and saving; the marginal propensity uses changes, not levels.
not.B: 0.40 is the MPS, the share of extra income saved.
not.D: 0.8 would need savings to rise by only 20 for each extra 100 of income.

2024-8.why: The Reserve Bank Board can decide and announce a change in the cash rate on the day it meets. The lag for monetary policy is in its effect, not its implementation.

not.A: Fiscal changes usually wait for the Budget and must pass Parliament.
not.C: Environmental policies need legislation, negotiation and long phase-in periods.
not.D: Microeconomic reforms take years to legislate and put in place.

2024-9.why: Frictional unemployment is people between jobs. Better job matching shortens the time it takes them to find work.

not.A: Better job search services would, if anything, encourage people to look for work, raising participation.
not.B: Faster matching would not reduce full-time employment.
not.C: Cyclical unemployment is caused by weak demand in a downturn, not by slow job matching.

2024-10.why: A higher cash rate attracts foreign savings, raising demand for the dollar, and buying Australian dollars in the foreign exchange market also raises demand. Both push the dollar up.

not.A: Selling Australian dollars increases their supply and pushes the dollar down.
not.C: Both actions push the dollar down.
not.D: Buying dollars supports the currency, but a lower cash rate reduces demand for it.

2024-11.why: Lower university fees lead to more people gaining skills. A more skilled workforce raises productive capacity, shifting aggregate supply to the right.

not.B: A higher GST raises prices and reduces spending; it does not increase productive capacity.
not.C: Fewer migrants means a smaller labour force, which would shift aggregate supply left.
not.D: Pension spending adds to consumption, which is aggregate demand, not supply.

2024-12.why: Capital account + financial account = 24 + 66 = 90, so the current account must be −90. Current account = (X − 36) + 12 − 120 − 6 = X − 150. Setting X − 150 = −90 gives X = $60 billion.

not.A: −$60 billion has the right size but exports of goods cannot be negative.
not.B: −$12 billion is not possible for exports and ignores the balancing of the accounts.
not.C: $54 billion leaves out net secondary income (−6).

2024-13.why: Local content rules require more locally made programs, so fewer foreign programs are imported and more local production jobs are created in the short term.

not.A: More local content replaces imported content, so imports fall rather than rise.
not.B: Imports fall, and local production needs more workers, not fewer.
not.D: Imports do fall, but short-term job opportunities in local production rise.

2024-14.why: A higher Gini coefficient means more inequality. Cutting childcare subsidies and lowering the tax-free threshold both take proportionally more from low-income households.

not.B: Raising the tax-free threshold helps low-income earners most, which reduces inequality.
not.C: Higher childcare subsidies help lower-income families work and earn more.
not.D: Both changes would reduce inequality, lowering the Gini coefficient.

2024-15.why: Net primary income is mostly interest and dividends paid overseas. Interest rates move with the cycle and change the cost of servicing foreign debt. Low national savings is the long-term (structural) reason Australia borrows from overseas at all.

not.A: The terms of trade mainly affect the balance on goods and services, and are not a structural factor.
not.C: The domestic business cycle is a cyclical factor, not a structural one.
not.D: A narrow export base and competitiveness are both structural, and they affect the goods and services balance.

2024-16.why: A cyclone that destroys fruit crops pushes fruit prices up sharply. Fruit is a volatile item: it is counted in headline inflation but removed from underlying inflation.

not.A: More oil production lowers fuel prices, which would pull headline inflation down.
not.B: Rising house prices are not a temporary, one-off price shock of the kind underlying inflation strips out.
not.C: A new shipping route lowers transport costs and prices.

2024-17.why: Paying more for imports means more Australian dollars are sold to buy foreign currency, which depreciates the dollar. Dearer inputs also raise firms' costs, so domestic prices rise.

not.A: Prices do rise, but a bigger import bill increases the supply of dollars, which lowers their value.
not.B: Both are the wrong direction.
not.D: The dollar does depreciate, but higher input costs raise prices, not lower them.

2024-18.why: The current account deficit was 35 ÷ 1200 = 2.92% of GDP in Year 1 and 36 ÷ 1250 = 2.88% in Year 2. A smaller deficit as a share of GDP is an improvement in external stability.

not.A: Net foreign liabilities did fall (900 to 850, or 75% to 68% of GDP), but that is an improvement, not a deterioration.
not.B: Net foreign liabilities as a share of GDP fell; they did not rise.
not.D: The deficit grew in dollars but shrank as a percentage of GDP.

2024-19.why: Weaker world demand for exports lowers export prices (terms of trade fall from 110 to 100) and lowers demand for the currency (TWI falls from 65 to 60).

not.A: Lower global inflation would make imports cheaper, which improves the terms of trade.
not.B: Higher domestic interest rates attract foreign funds and push the TWI up.
not.C: Domestic unemployment does not directly change export or import prices.

not.A: Growth is right, but 10 is the rise in index points; as a percentage of 110 it is 9.1%.
not.C: 12.5% is nominal GDP growth, and 10 is index points, not the inflation rate.
not.D: Inflation is right, but 12.5% is nominal growth with price rises still included.

2023-1.why: The OECD is a group of mostly advanced economies that share research and coordinate policy to support sustainable growth, employment and living standards in its members.

not.A: Low-interest and interest-free development loans come from the World Bank.
not.C: Supporting liquidity in a financial crisis is the role of the IMF.
not.D: A forum of the seven largest advanced economies is the G7.

2023-2.why: Mining (iron ore, coal, gas) is by far Australia's largest export earner by value.

not.A: Manufacturing is a small and declining share of Australia's exports.
not.C: Rural exports are significant but far smaller than mining.
not.D: Services (education, tourism) are important but well below mining in value.

2023-3.why: Keeping 16 and 17 year olds at school removes them from the labour force while they are still counted in the working age population (15 and over), so the participation rate falls.

not.A: Higher GDP creates jobs and draws people into the labour force.
not.B: More childcare places make it easier for parents to work, raising participation.
not.D: A later retirement age keeps older workers in the labour force, raising participation.

2023-4.why: AD has shifted to the right. Lower taxes raise disposable income and consumption, increasing aggregate demand.

not.B: Imports are a leakage: more imports reduce aggregate demand.
not.C: Lower consumption shifts AD to the left.
not.D: Capacity constraints limit aggregate supply; they do not shift AD to the right.

2023-5.why: A tariff raises the price of imported farm products for Country A's consumers. Country B's farmers sell less to Country A, so their income falls.

not.A: Prices do rise in Country A, but exporters in Country B lose sales and income.
not.C: A tariff makes imports dearer, not cheaper, and it does not help Country B's producers.
not.D: Country B's producers do lose income, but prices in Country A rise.

2023-6.why: Free trade lets resources move to industries where Australia has a comparative advantage and opens larger markets, lifting productivity and long-run real GDP.

not.A: Agreements favour members, so trade can be diverted away from non-members.
not.B: Removing tariffs reduces tariff revenue.
not.D: Less competitive industries shrink at first, which raises structural unemployment in the short term.

2023-7.why: A public good is non-excludable and non-rival: no one can be stopped from breathing clean air, and one person's use does not reduce another's.

not.B: Public housing is excludable and rival: a home given to one family is not available to another.
not.C: Internet access is excludable (you pay for a connection).
not.D: Bus travel is excludable by fare and seats are rival, even when the government provides it.

2023-8.why: A contractionary stance takes more out of the economy than before. Moving from a $10 million to a $20 million surplus does that.

not.A: A smaller surplus means the budget is taking less out of the economy: expansionary.
not.B: The outcome has not changed, so the stance is unchanged.
not.C: A larger deficit is more expansionary.

2023-9.why: A rising HDI means better health, education and income. Greater access to transport and communication is a mark of development and of integration with the global economy.

not.A: More protection cuts an economy off from trade and usually slows development.
not.B: Less access to technology would hold back education and income.
not.D: Lower financial flows mean less investment, which slows development.

2023-10.why: A smaller quota lets in fewer imports. One reason to restrict imports is to stop foreign firms dumping goods at below-cost prices on the local market.

not.B: Fewer imports would increase a current account surplus, not reduce it.
not.C: Protection raises prices and reduces choice, lowering living standards.
not.D: Protection shelters less efficient industries; it works against specialisation by comparative advantage.

2023-11.why: The supply of Australian dollars has decreased (S1 to S2 is a shift left). Australians supply dollars when they buy imports, so lower demand for imports reduces supply.

not.A: Higher commodity prices increase the demand for Australian dollars; they do not reduce supply.
not.B: Lower Australian interest rates send funds overseas, which increases the supply of dollars.
not.D: Fewer investment opportunities reduce foreign demand for dollars, and may increase supply as Australians invest abroad.

2023-12.why: A lower cash rate lowers borrowing costs. Cheaper credit raises demand for assets such as houses and shares, lifting their prices, and makes more business investment worthwhile.

not.A: Both are the wrong direction: these are the effects of a higher cash rate.
not.B: Investment does rise, but cheaper credit pushes asset prices up, not down.
not.C: Asset prices do rise, but lower borrowing costs increase investment.

2023-13.why: Net foreign liabilities = all foreign liabilities minus all foreign assets. Liabilities: loans owed to foreigners 1200 + Country X assets owned by foreigners 500 = 1700. Assets: loans owed by foreigners 300 + foreign assets owned 200 = 500. 1700 − 500 = $1200 billion.

not.A: $600 billion does not come from the four items: all the liabilities must be added before all the assets are taken away.
not.B: $800 billion subtracts items that should be added: foreign-owned assets in Country X are a liability.
not.C: $900 billion is net foreign debt only (1200 − 300). Net foreign equity (500 − 200) has been left out.

2023-14.why: Producers ignore the external cost they impose on others. A tax adds that cost to their own costs, raising marginal private cost towards marginal social cost so that less is produced.

not.B: Lowering private cost would encourage even more production.
not.C: The tax is on producers' costs; it does not change the benefit buyers receive.
not.D: The problem is on the cost side of production, not the benefit side.

2023-15.why: Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Export prices falling while import prices rise makes the ratio fall sharply.

not.B: If both fall by the same percentage the ratio does not change.
not.C: Export prices up and import prices down is an improvement.
not.D: If both rise by the same percentage the ratio does not change.

2023-16.why: The rate is fixed at 0.50, below the market equilibrium of 0.75. At 0.50 demand for the currency exceeds supply, so the central bank must supply more of its own currency by selling it and buying foreign currency.

not.A: Higher interest rates would attract funds and push the currency further above the fixed rate.
not.C: Buying the domestic currency adds to demand and pushes its value up.
not.D: Restricting outflows reduces the supply of the currency, pushing its value up.

2023-17.why: Contribution = weight × price rise. Education 15 × 15 = 225; Food 35 × 10 = 350; Health 20 × 25 = 500; Housing 16 × 30 = 480. Health is the largest.

not.A: Education has the smallest contribution (225).
not.B: Food has the largest weight but the smallest price rise (350).
not.D: Housing has the largest price rise but a smaller weight than Health (480).

2023-18.why: Income rose by 100 and consumption by 80, so MPC = 0.8 and the multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 5. Extra income = 5 × 50 = 250, so national income = 1100 + 250 = $1350 million.

not.A: $1150 million just adds the $50 million with no multiplier.
not.B: $1200 million uses a multiplier of 2.
not.D: $1600 million uses a multiplier of 10.

2023-19.why: At the world price of $5, domestic supply is 50 000 and demand is 150 000, so imports are 100 000. A subsidy does not change the price consumers pay, so to cut imports by 50 000 domestic supply must rise to 100 000. Producers supply 100 000 only at $15, so the subsidy is $15 − $5 = $10.

not.A: A $5 subsidy gives producers $10, at which they supply 75 000: imports fall by only 25 000.
not.C: $15 is the price producers need to receive, not the subsidy on top of the $5 world price.
not.D: A $20 subsidy would lift supply to 150 000 and end imports altogether.

2023-20.why: The TWI weights each currency by its share of trade. A 10% fall against the yen (weight 13) outweighs a 10% rise against the US dollar (weight 8), so the index falls.

not.A: The rise against the renminbi (31) far outweighs the fall against the euro (9): the TWI rises.
not.B: The rise against the yen (13) outweighs the fall against the won (7): the TWI rises.
not.C: The rise against the euro (9) slightly outweighs the fall against the US dollar (8): the TWI rises a little.

2022-1.why: The IMF oversees the international monetary system and lends to countries in financial difficulty to keep the global financial system stable.

not.A: The World Bank funds development projects to reduce poverty.
not.B: The United Nations deals with peace, security and development, not financial stability.
not.D: The OECD researches and coordinates economic policy among its members.

2022-2.why: To be unemployed a person must be actively looking for work. Someone who has given up looking is a discouraged (hidden unemployed) worker: not counted as unemployed and not in the labour force.

not.B: The labour force is the employed plus the unemployed; this person is neither.
not.C: A person cannot be unemployed without being in the labour force.
not.D: They are no longer actively seeking work, so they are not counted as unemployed.

2022-3.why: Transnational corporations drive trade and investment across borders, so a decline in their significance would slow globalisation.

not.A: Migration moves labour between economies, which is part of globalisation.
not.B: Larger financial flows link economies more closely.
not.C: Lower protection increases trade.

2022-4.why: Full employment is the lowest rate of unemployment that does not cause inflation to accelerate (the NAIRU). Some frictional and structural unemployment remains.

not.A: There are always people between jobs, so unemployment is never zero.
not.B: At full employment there is no cyclical unemployment.
not.C: Frictional unemployment also remains, not only structural.

2022-5.why: A lower currency means more local currency is needed to buy the same imports, so import prices rise and feed into inflation.

not.A: Imports become dearer, not cheaper.
not.C: Exports do become cheaper for foreign buyers, but dearer imports and stronger demand add to inflation.
not.D: A depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers, not more expensive.

2022-6.why: Tradable permits create a market for the right to use water, so the price of permits rations use. That is a market-based policy.

not.A: A target is a goal, such as an emissions level by a set year.
not.B: A regulation is a direct rule or ban, with no buying and selling.
not.D: This is a domestic scheme, not an agreement between countries.

2022-7.why: Buying shares worth $1 million in a large bank is well under 10% of the company, so it is not direct investment. NESA accepted both portfolio investment and other investment for this question.

not.A: Direct investment needs a holding of 10% or more, giving a say in running the company.
not.C: Financial derivatives are contracts such as futures and options, not shares.

2022-8.why: AD has shifted to the left. Exports are an injection: an increase in exports would shift AD to the right, so it cannot be the cause.

not.B: More imports are a leakage that reduces AD, so this could cause the shift.
not.C: Lower business investment reduces AD, so this could cause the shift.
not.D: Lower government spending reduces AD, so this could cause the shift.

2022-9.why: A wage subsidy is government spending. Ending it lowers spending and so reduces the budget deficit.

not.A: Removing support is contractionary; it does not expand the economy.
not.C: Ending a spending program would increase a surplus, not reduce it.
not.D: Discouraging hiring is a side effect a government would want to avoid, not a reason.

2022-10.why: Blocking a merger is a rule applied by government (regulation), and airlines sell a service to consumers, so the market is a product market.

not.A: Factor markets are for inputs such as labour and capital, not air travel.
not.C: Stopping a merger is regulation, and this is not a factor market.
not.D: It is a product market, but the government is intervening, which is regulation rather than deregulation.

2022-11.why: Current account = net goods + net services + primary income + secondary income = 80.5 + 10.2 − 63.8 − 4.3 = $22.6 billion (a surplus).

not.B: The size is right but the sign is wrong: the positive goods and services balance is larger than the income deficits.
not.C: $30.7 billion is the size of the capital and financial account (13.2 + 17.5).
not.D: −$30.7 billion is the capital and financial account, not the current account.

2022-12.why: The GST is regressive: lower-income households spend a larger share of their income, so a higher rate takes proportionally more from them. Inequality rises, which is a higher Gini coefficient.

not.A: A higher GST widens inequality; it does not reduce it.
not.B: A lower Gini coefficient means more equality, so this option contradicts itself.
not.C: A higher Gini coefficient means more inequality, so this option contradicts itself.

2022-13.why: Cheaper childcare makes paid work worthwhile for more parents, so more of them join the labour force.

not.A: A lower tax-free threshold means tax is paid on more income, reducing the reward for working.
not.C: A higher top marginal rate reduces the incentive to work.
not.D: Keeping young people at school longer takes them out of the labour force.

2022-14.why: AD shifting left and AS shifting left both reduce output, so GDP falls for certain.

not.A: Both shifts to the right raise GDP.
not.B: AD right raises output while AS left lowers it: the result is uncertain.
not.C: AD left lowers output while AS right raises it: the result is uncertain.

2022-15.why: The NAIRU depends on structural and frictional unemployment. Training gives the unemployed the skills employers want, lowering structural unemployment.

not.A: Interest rates affect cyclical unemployment, not the NAIRU.
not.B: Higher company tax discourages investment and hiring.
not.C: Higher welfare payments can reduce the incentive to seek work, which may raise the NAIRU.

2022-16.why: Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ CPI × 100. Country C: 23 ÷ 118 × 100 = 19.5, below the $20 billion of Year 1, so real growth is negative.

2021-1.why: The WTO administers the rules of world trade and runs a dispute settlement process for members.

not.B: Low-interest loans come from the World Bank and the IMF.
not.C: Countries set their own tariffs and subsidies; the WTO provides a forum to negotiate limits on them.
not.D: Trading blocs are formed by the countries themselves.

2021-2.why: High income per person and a diversified (wide) export base are features of an advanced economy. Population size is not part of the classification.

not.A: Emerging economies are industrialising quickly but have middle incomes.
not.C: Developing economies have low incomes and usually a narrow export base.
not.D: An economic forum is a group of countries, such as the G20, not a type of economy.

not.B: Public holidays are one of the National Employment Standards.
not.D: The right to request flexible working arrangements is one of the National Employment Standards.

not.B: Revenue does fall, but less revenue makes a deficit bigger.
not.C: Tax revenue falls in a downturn; it does not rise.
not.D: Both are the wrong direction.

2021-5.why: The structural component is what the budget balance would be with the effect of the business cycle removed, so it shows the government's deliberate decisions.

not.A: The cyclical component changes automatically with the level of economic activity.
not.C: The headline cash balance is a measure of the total outcome, including both components.
not.D: The underlying cash balance is also a measure of the total outcome, not of policy decisions alone.

2021-6.why: A higher Gini coefficient means more inequality. A consumption tax is regressive: it takes a larger share of income from low-income earners.

not.C: Training raises workers' skills and wages, which tends to reduce inequality.
not.D: Welfare spending goes mostly to low-income households, reducing inequality.

not.A: Changing tax rates is a deliberate (discretionary) decision.
not.B: Infrastructure spending is a discretionary decision.
not.C: Changing benefit rates is a discretionary decision. The stabiliser is the number of people receiving benefits.

2021-8.why: A larger quota allows more imports and lower tariffs make them cheaper: both reduce protection.

not.A: Higher tariffs increase protection.
not.B: Export incentives are a form of protection, so increasing them moves away from free trade.
not.D: A smaller quota allows fewer imports, which is more protection.

2021-9.why: Cheaper imports reduce import payments, and a depreciation makes exports more competitive and imports less attractive. Both improve the current account.

not.A: Lower net saving means more borrowing from overseas, which worsens the current account.
not.C: Higher export prices help, but higher debt servicing costs enlarge the primary income deficit.
not.D: More business investment usually means more imports of capital goods and more foreign borrowing.

2021-10.why: From X to Y the economy is slowing. Contractionary policy does that: higher taxes (fiscal) and a higher cash rate (monetary) both reduce spending.

not.B: Both are expansionary and would lift GDP.

not.A: More saving is a larger leakage; neither income nor the multiplier rises.
not.B: The multiplier does fall, but so does income.
not.C: Income does fall, but the multiplier falls too.

2021-13.why: Public goods are non-excludable, so people can use them without paying directly. This is why they are funded from taxation.

2021-14.why: Money sent home by migrant workers is a transfer with nothing received in return, so it is secondary income. Money leaving Australia is a debit.

not.A: Primary income is earnings such as wages, interest and dividends, not gifts.
not.B: It is neither primary income nor an inflow.
not.D: It is secondary income, but an outflow is a debit.

2021-15.why: A higher minimum wage attracts more people into the labour force (participation rises), but employers demand less labour at the higher wage, so more of them are unemployed.

not.B: Higher government spending creates jobs and lowers the unemployment rate.
not.C: Hidden unemployed people have left the labour force, so participation falls.
not.D: A higher school leaving age takes young people out of the labour force.

2021-16.why: An externality falls on people outside the transaction. Faster trips are the benefit drivers pay the toll for, so they are a private benefit.

not.A: Noise affects nearby residents who are not users: a negative externality.

2021-17.why: Unemployment rate: 2.5 ÷ 13.6 = 18.4% in Year 1, 2.3 ÷ 14.3 = 16.1% in Year 2 (decreased). Participation rate: 13.6 ÷ 25 = 54.4%, then 14.3 ÷ 26 = 55.0% (increased).

2021-19.why: Stronger demand has pushed the currency above the range. Lowering the cash rate makes the currency less attractive to foreign savers, reducing demand and bringing its value down.

2020-1.why: The Reserve Bank's objectives include the stability of the currency (low inflation) and the maintenance of full employment.

not.B: External stability is not an objective of monetary policy.
not.C: Distribution of income is pursued mainly through fiscal policy.
not.D: Environmental sustainability is not an objective of monetary policy.

2020-2.why: The IMF monitors the global financial system and lends to countries in crisis to maintain financial stability.

not.A: The World Bank funds long-term development.
not.B: The WTO deals with the rules of trade.
not.D: APEC is a regional forum promoting trade and cooperation in the Asia-Pacific.

2020-3.why: In a decentralised system wages and conditions are negotiated at each workplace, so agreements differ between workplaces.

not.A: Decentralised bargaining tends to widen wage differences.
not.B: Linking wages to inflation (indexation) is a feature of centralised wage fixing.

2020-4.why: Developing economies lack the income and tax base to fund schools and public goods such as roads, sanitation and power.

not.A: Productivity is low, but population growth is usually high.
not.B: Infant mortality is high in developing economies.
not.D: Health care is inadequate, but their GDP is usually dominated by agriculture, not services.

2020-5.why: A smaller quota means less wheat can be imported. Total supply in the country falls, so the price rises.

not.B: Foreign exporters sell less wheat, so their revenue falls.
not.C: Local producers sell more at a higher price, so their income rises.
not.D: A quota is a limit on quantity; unlike a tariff it does not raise revenue from each unit imported.

not.A: 50 is right, but that is a fall from 80.

not.A: Australia is selling the rights and receiving payment, which is a credit, not a debit.
not.D: NESA did not accept this option: the sale of the rights itself is recorded as a credit in the capital account, not the financial account.

2020-8.why: Hidden unemployed people have stopped looking for work, so they are no longer in the labour force. More of them means a lower participation rate.

not.A: Lower unemployment signals that jobs are available and tends to draw people into the labour force.
not.B: Fewer discouraged workers means more people are back in the labour force.
not.D: To receive unemployment payments people must be looking for work, which keeps them in the labour force.

2020-9.why: AD2 is to the left of AD1, so aggregate demand has fallen. A higher cash rate raises borrowing costs and reduces consumption and investment.

not.A: A higher tax-free threshold leaves households more income, raising AD.
not.B: More business investment raises AD.
not.D: More employment in a trading partner raises its demand for exports, raising AD.

2020-10.why: The CPI rose 3% and the unemployment rate fell from 10% (200 ÷ 2000) to 5.9% (125 ÷ 2125). Stronger consumer confidence raises spending and prices. A higher currency in a trading partner makes this economy's exports cheaper there, creating jobs.

not.A: A lower cash rate could raise the CPI, but removing training programs would raise unemployment.
not.B: An appreciation makes imports cheaper, which lowers the CPI.
not.C: A global downturn would raise unemployment, not lower it.

2020-11.why: Lower interest rates (an expansionary stance) reduce demand for the currency, so it depreciates. Loans in foreign currencies then cost more to service and repay in local currency.

not.A: The stance is right, but a weaker currency makes buying assets overseas more expensive.
not.C: A contractionary stance raises interest rates and appreciates the currency.
not.D: A contractionary stance would appreciate the currency, not depreciate it.

2020-12.why: Growth rose but the unemployment rate stayed at 5.2%, the NAIRU. Stronger demand was met by existing workers getting more hours, so underemployment fell without changing the unemployment rate.

not.A: Lower aggregate supply would not produce faster growth.
not.B: Lower aggregate supply would not produce faster growth.
not.D: A fall in structural unemployment would have lowered the unemployment rate, which did not change.

2020-13.why: Higher returns on Australian-owned investments overseas increase income from abroad and the value of foreign assets, which reduces net foreign liabilities.

not.A: Higher debt servicing costs add to the current account deficit and to liabilities.
not.B: Exchange rate volatility does not in itself reduce liabilities.
not.C: More foreign investment into the economy increases foreign liabilities.

2019-1.why: Globalisation lets firms split production across countries, with each stage done where it is cheapest: the international division of labour.

not.B: Globalisation is associated with lower, not higher, protection.
not.C: More integrated markets are generally more efficient.
not.D: Globalisation is increased economic integration.

2019-2.why: The G20 brings together leaders, finance ministers and central bank governors of major economies to coordinate economic policy.

not.A: It has no preferential trade arrangements, so it is not a trading bloc.

not.C: Its members keep their own currencies.

not.A: A larger trade deficit is a cost of an appreciation, not a benefit.
not.B: Imports become cheaper, so import volumes rise.
not.D: An appreciation makes exports dearer, reducing competitiveness.

2019-4.why: Monetary policy is set by the Reserve Bank, which is independent of the government, so it is the least exposed to political pressure.

not.A: Budgets must pass Parliament and are shaped by elections.

2019-5.why: Parents returning to work move from outside the labour force into it, raising the participation rate.

not.D: Full-time students are generally not in the labour force.

not.A: With low inflation, workers need and seek smaller pay rises.
not.C: Weak growth means weak demand for labour.
not.D: Without productivity gains firms cannot afford larger pay rises.

2019-8.why: Mining (iron ore, coal, gas) is the largest export sector and services (education, tourism) the next largest.

2018-2.why: The World Bank lends to developing economies for infrastructure and other development projects.

not.B: The WTO oversees trade rules and does not lend.

not.D: The OECD is a policy forum of mostly advanced economies.

2018-4.why: A lower company tax rate raises after-tax returns, making the country more attractive to foreign firms deciding where to invest.

not.A: More investment inflow raises demand for the currency, appreciating it.
not.B: Lower tax increases after-tax profit.
not.C: Company tax has no direct link to people moving between jobs.

2018-5.why: Exports become more competitive when the currency falls. Buying foreign currency means selling the domestic currency (more supply), and lower interest rates reduce demand for it.

not.A: Selling the currency lowers it, but higher interest rates push it back up.
not.B: Both actions raise the currency.
not.C: Lower rates help, but selling foreign currency means buying the domestic currency, which raises it.

2018-6.why: Each extra user reduces the speed available to others. That is rivalry in consumption.

not.A: Redundancy pay is one of the National Employment Standards.
not.B: Four weeks annual leave is one of the National Employment Standards.
not.C: Notice of termination is one of the National Employment Standards.

2018-11.why: Moving from a $10 billion surplus to a $5 billion deficit means the budget is now adding to demand: an expansionary stance.

not.A: A larger surplus is contractionary.

not.C: Moving from deficit to surplus is contractionary.

2018-12.why: Firms that operate across state borders faced a different set of rules in each state. One national system gives them a single set.

2018-13.why: Rules such as competition law stop firms abusing market power, which makes markets work more efficiently.

not.A: Many regulations improve efficiency by correcting market failure.

not.D: Regulation is not generally aimed at keeping transnational corporations out.

2018-14.why: Most people earn wages as employees. Returns to enterprise (profit) go to the smaller number who run businesses, and many small businesses earn little.

2018-15.why: In Year 2 households consume less at every level of income. Higher interest rates reward saving and raise loan repayments, reducing consumption.

not.A: Higher asset prices make households feel wealthier and spend more.
not.C: Lower unemployment raises confidence and spending.

2018-16.why: Stronger world demand for this economy's exports raises export prices relative to import prices (terms of trade up) and raises demand for its currency (TWI up).

not.B: A higher cash rate would lift the TWI but would not change the terms of trade.
not.C: Stronger demand for the goods it imports would raise import prices and worsen the terms of trade.

2018-17.why: More oil production lowers petrol prices. Petrol is a volatile item counted in headline inflation but excluded from underlying, so headline falls below underlying.

not.A: Less electricity production raises power prices.

not.C: Injections (115) are less than leakages (125).

2013-8.why: The NAIRU reflects structural unemployment. Retraining gives job seekers the skills employers need, reducing the mismatch.

not.D: Infrastructure spending mainly reduces cyclical unemployment.

2013-9.why: Producers ignore the external cost, so the market price is below the true social cost and too much is produced.

not.A: The price is too low because it leaves out the external cost.
not.B: Output is too high, not too low.
not.D: This describes a positive externality.

2013-10.why: Current account = 100 − 120 − 140 − 40 = −200. With a floating exchange rate a current account deficit of $200 billion is matched by a surplus of $200 billion on the capital and financial account.

not.A: $160 billion leaves out net secondary income, and the balance is a surplus.

2013-11.why: Seasonal unemployment follows the time of year, such as fruit picking. It is not affected by the long-term shift from manufacturing to mining.

not.B: Workers moving between industries spend time between jobs.
not.C: A change in the structure of industry is the cause of structural unemployment.
not.D: Displaced manufacturing workers without the right skills can be out of work for long periods.

2013-12.why: More and better machinery lets each worker produce more.

not.A: Income tax rates do not change what a firm's workers can produce.
not.C: Lower demand reduces sales, not output per worker.
not.D: A smaller quota gives more protection and less pressure to improve.

2013-13.why: Selling foreign currency means buying Australian dollars, adding to demand. A higher cash rate attracts foreign funds, also adding to demand.

not.A: Buying foreign currency means selling Australian dollars, which lowers the dollar.

not.D: Both actions lower the dollar.

2013-14.why: Lower interest rates raise consumption and investment. A lower dollar makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, raising net exports.

not.A: Both changes reduce aggregate demand.
not.C: Lower rates help, but an appreciation reduces net exports.
not.D: A depreciation helps, but higher rates reduce spending.

2013-15.why: The multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − MPC). A lower MPC means a smaller multiplier, and with less consumption equilibrium income falls.

not.A: Both are the wrong direction.
not.C: The multiplier does fall, but so does income.
not.D: A lower MPC reduces the multiplier.

2013-16.why: Lower Australian rates lead investors to sell Australian dollars and move funds overseas. The supply of dollars rises and the dollar falls against trading partners' currencies.

not.A: A greater supply of dollars lowers the TWI.

not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

2013-17.why: Selling securities takes cash out of the banking system, reducing the money supply and pushing interest rates up.

not.A: Buying securities adds cash: expansionary.
not.C: Selling securities reduces the money supply.
not.D: Buying securities increases the money supply.

2013-18.why: More oil lowers petrol prices. Petrol is a volatile item that is counted in headline inflation but excluded from underlying.

not.A: Established house prices are not in the CPI.

not.C: Less oil would raise petrol prices and headline inflation.

2013-19.why: Terms of trade = export prices ÷ import prices × 100 = 110 ÷ 105 × 100 = 104.8, a rise from 100. Net export volume goes from 100 − 100 = 0 to 105 − 110 = −5, a decrease.

not.A: The terms of trade rose, but import volumes grew faster than export volumes.
not.B: Export prices rose more than import prices, so the terms of trade rose.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

2013-20.why: With a $10 tariff the price is $30, the no-trade equilibrium: no imports, no revenue, and local output of 100. With a $5 tariff the price is $25: local output falls to 90 and imports are 20, so revenue rises to 20 × $5 = $100.

not.A: Revenue rises, but a lower price reduces local output.
not.B: Local output falls, but revenue rises from zero.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

2012-1.why: The EU is a group of countries with free trade among members and common barriers to others.

not.A: The UN is concerned with peace, security and development.
not.C: The G20 is a forum for policy coordination.
not.D: The OECD is a policy research forum.

2012-2.why: The Fair Work system replaced thousands of state and federal awards with a much smaller number of modern awards.

not.B: Enterprise agreements remain central to the system.
not.C: The minimum wage is reviewed each year and was not reduced.
not.D: The safety net was kept through the National Employment Standards and modern awards.

2012-3.why: Development brings better education, health and capital, all of which raise output per worker.

not.A: Education levels rise with development.
not.C: Reliance on aid falls as incomes rise.
not.D: Agriculture shrinks as a share of GDP as industry and services grow.

2012-4.why: The Reserve Bank's charter refers to the stability of the currency, full employment and the economic prosperity and welfare of the people.

not.B: National debt is a matter for fiscal policy.
not.C: National savings are not an objective of monetary policy.
not.D: Income distribution is addressed mainly through fiscal policy.

2012-5.why: Output has fallen and unemployment has risen to 8%. Both policies should stimulate demand to create jobs.

not.B: Contractionary fiscal policy would cost jobs.
not.C: Contractionary monetary policy would cost jobs.
not.D: Both would raise unemployment further.

2012-6.why: Labour force = employed + unemployed. Year 1: 200 000 + 600 000 + 100 000 = 900 000. Year 2: 210 000 + 640 000 + 110 000 = 960 000. The change is 60 000.

not.A: 40 000 is the change in full-time employment only.
not.B: 50 000 is the change in total employment; the unemployed are also in the labour force.

not.A: Exports (80) exceed imports (70): a trade surplus.
not.C: Injections (40 + 50 + 80 = 170) equal leakages (40 + 60 + 70 = 170).

2012-8.why: Fewer people in work means less income tax, and more people out of work means more unemployment benefits.

not.A: Income tax revenue falls when fewer people have jobs.
not.B: Social security payments rise with unemployment.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

2012-9.why: Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper and saving less rewarding, so households spend more and save a smaller share of income.

not.A: Spending rises when rates fall.
not.B: A lower return on saving reduces the saving rate.
not.C: Both are the wrong direction.

2012-10.why: Banks pay for the securities from their exchange settlement accounts, so cash becomes scarcer and the cash rate rises.

not.A: Less cash pushes interest rates up.
not.B: Selling securities removes cash.
not.D: Selling securities removes cash from the accounts.

not.A: $900bn would give a current account surplus of 200.

not.D: $300bn would give a deficit of 400.

2012-12.why: A subsidy encourages activities with benefits to others, and a tax makes polluters pay for the costs they impose.

not.A: Taxing a positive externality discourages a beneficial activity.
not.B: Subsidising a negative externality encourages a harmful activity.
not.C: This rewards harm and penalises benefit.

2012-13.why: Public goods are non-excludable: people cannot be charged at the point of use, so they are funded from taxation.

not.A: They are not priced in a market at all.
not.B: Their supply is decided by government and is not fixed.
not.C: People cannot be made to pay directly, which is why markets do not provide them.

2012-14.why: AS has shifted to the right. Higher labour productivity lowers the cost of each unit of output and raises productive capacity.

not.A: The budget balance affects aggregate demand.
not.C: A higher minimum wage raises costs, shifting AS to the left.
not.D: Interest rates affect aggregate demand.

2012-15.why: Year 1: labour force 24 million; participation 24 ÷ 30 = 80%; unemployment 3 ÷ 24 = 12.5%. Year 2: labour force 30 million; participation 30 ÷ 40 = 75%; unemployment 3 ÷ 30 = 10%. Both are lower.

not.B: Unemployment falls from 12.5% to 10%.
not.C: Participation falls from 80% to 75%.
not.D: Both rates fall.

2012-16.why: When national savings fall short of investment, the gap is funded from overseas, and the cost of servicing that borrowing adds to the current account deficit.

not.C: A larger budget surplus adds to national savings.
not.D: Overseas students are an export of services.

2012-17.why: One Australian dollar buys more euros (0.7 to 0.8), so it appreciated against the euro. It buys fewer US dollars (1.10 to 1.00), so it depreciated against the US dollar.

not.A: It buys more yen (80 to 90), so it appreciated against the yen.
not.B: It appreciated against the euro.
not.D: It appreciated against the euro and depreciated against the US dollar.

2012-18.why: The subsidy is the vertical gap between the two supply curves. At the quantity of 20, producers need $12 without the subsidy (S1) but accept $10 with it (S2): a subsidy of $2.

2012-19.why: The multiplier is 20 000 ÷ 5000 = 4. Since k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC), 1 − MPC = 0.25 and MPC = 0.75.

not.A: An MPC of 0.2 gives a multiplier of 1.25.
not.B: 0.25 is the MPS.
not.D: An MPC of 0.8 gives a multiplier of 5.

2012-20.why: In a recession households and firms buy less of everything, including imports. A depreciation makes imports dearer.

not.A: A recession reduces imports, but an appreciation makes them cheaper.

not.C: Both changes increase imports.

2011-1.why: Dearer oil raises the cost of transporting goods around the world, which discourages trade.

not.A: Workers moving more freely between countries speeds up globalisation.
not.B: Cheaper communication speeds up globalisation.
not.D: Lower export subsidies are a reduction in protection, which frees up trade.

2011-2.why: A higher minimum wage lifts the incomes of the lowest-paid workers, narrowing the gap with higher earners.

not.B: Lower benefits reduce the incomes of the poorest households.
not.C: Decentralised bargaining tends to widen wage differences.
not.D: Less education and training reduces the earning power of lower-income people.

2011-3.why: More competition in labour and other factor markets makes wages and employment more flexible, reducing structural unemployment and so the NAIRU.

not.A: Fiscal policy acts on cyclical unemployment, not the NAIRU.
not.B: Monetary policy acts on cyclical unemployment, not the NAIRU.
not.D: Less competition makes the economy less efficient.

2011-4.why: Injections = G + I + X = 30 + 25 + 30 = 85. Withdrawals = S + T + M = 30 + 20 + 35 = 85. They are equal, so income is in equilibrium.

not.A: Income contracts only when withdrawals exceed injections.
not.B: Both total 85.
not.C: Both total 85.

2011-5.why: AS has shifted to the left. Higher labour costs per unit of output make production dearer at every price level.

not.B: Lower inflationary expectations restrain wage claims, shifting AS right.
not.C: A change in national income is a movement along the curves, not a shift of AS.
not.D: An appreciation lowers the cost of imported inputs, shifting AS right.

2011-6.why: An appreciation makes Australian exports dearer for foreign buyers, and a US recession reduces their demand.

not.A: A depreciation makes exports cheaper, working against the effect of the recession.
not.C: Both changes increase exports.
not.D: An appreciation hurts, but a US expansion raises demand.

2011-7.why: The terms of trade have fallen (110 to 105), reducing export income and economic activity. Higher government spending offsets the fall in demand.

not.A: Higher interest rates would slow the economy further.
not.B: Higher taxes would slow the economy further.
not.D: A higher currency would make exports even less competitive.

2011-8.why: Asset prices such as property and shares tend to rise with inflation, so the owners' wealth keeps its real value or grows.

not.B: A fixed income buys less as prices rise.
not.C: The real value of money in the bank falls.
not.D: Pensioners are on low, largely fixed incomes that lag behind price rises.

2011-9.why: More inequality means more low-income households needing support, which costs the government more.

not.A: Faster growth would be a benefit, not a cost.
not.B: Greater mobility of labour is a benefit of wider wage differences.
not.C: More risk-taking is a benefit of larger rewards.

2011-10.why: Supply of Australian dollars has decreased. A smaller net income deficit means fewer dollars are sold to pay interest and dividends overseas.

not.A: More imports mean more dollars are supplied.
not.B: Foreign investment in Australia changes the demand for dollars, not the supply.
not.D: Less competitive firms mean more imports, increasing supply.

2011-11.why: Higher returns in Australia attract foreign funds. Investors must buy Australian dollars, so demand rises and the dollar appreciates.

not.A: More capital inflow raises the dollar.
not.C: Higher relative rates attract investment.
not.D: The dollar does appreciate, but because foreign investment rises.

2011-12.why: In an expansion incomes rise, so more income tax is collected, and unemployment falls, so fewer benefits are paid.

not.A: Unemployment benefits fall when more people have jobs.
not.B: Tax receipts rise with incomes.
not.C: This describes a downturn.

2011-13.why: Income rose by 150 and consumption by 90, so MPC = 0.6 and the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5. Extra income = 2.5 × 40 = 100, so Y = 300 + 100 = $400bn.

not.A: $360bn uses a multiplier of 1.5.
not.B: $367bn uses a multiplier of 1 ÷ 0.6 instead of 1 ÷ 0.4.
not.D: $420bn uses a multiplier of 3.

2011-14.why: A current account deficit is financed by borrowing or selling assets, adding to liabilities. A depreciation raises the Australian dollar value of debt owed in foreign currencies.

not.A: An appreciation reduces the value of foreign currency debt.
not.C: A surplus reduces liabilities.
not.D: A surplus reduces liabilities.

2011-15.why: Current account = −15 + 5 − 50 + 5 = −55. The capital and financial account must be +55. With a capital account of 5, the financial account is 55 − 5 = $50bn.

not.A: $45bn leaves out one of the current account items.
not.C: $55bn is the whole capital and financial account.
not.D: $60bn adds the capital account instead of subtracting it.

2011-16.why: Lower government spending reduces demand, and selling securities takes cash out of the system and raises interest rates. Both are contractionary.

not.A: Lower taxes increase spending.
not.C: Buying securities lowers interest rates.
not.D: Both would add to inflation.

2011-17.why: At $10: demand 400, local supply 100, imports 300, so foreign revenue is 300 × $10 = $3000. With the tariff the price is $15: demand 300, local supply 200, imports 100. Foreign producers still receive $10, so revenue is $1000. The fall is $2000.

not.A: $500 is the tariff revenue (100 × $5).
not.B: $1000 is foreign producers' revenue after the tariff, not the fall.
not.C: $1500 is what consumers pay for imports after the tariff (100 × $15).

2011-18.why: The HDI combines income, life expectancy and education. Country A has a lower income but a higher HDI, so it must score higher on health and education.

not.A: The HDI says nothing about how income is distributed.
not.B: The HDI says nothing about how income is distributed.
not.C: With lower income and lower health and education, A's HDI would be lower.

2011-19.why: Borrowing from the central bank creates new money to pay for the spending, adding directly to demand.

not.A: Selling assets raises funds without creating money.
not.C: Borrowing existing savings does not add to the money supply and pushes interest rates up.
not.D: Borrowing overseas does not create new money at home.

2011-20.why: Adding the social cost to firms' costs shifts supply to the left: less is produced and the price is higher.

not.A: Higher costs raise the price.
not.B: Higher costs reduce output.
not.D: This would happen if costs fell.

2010-1.why: Producing more output needs more workers, so growth and employment rise together.

not.A: Strong growth tends to push prices up.
not.B: Strong growth draws in imports, worsening the external balance.
not.D: More production usually means more resource use and pollution.

2010-2.why: National Competition Policy increased competition among firms selling goods and services.

not.A: Labour is a factor of production, so this is a factor market.
not.B: Income tax changes affect incentives to work, a labour market matter.
not.C: Finance (capital) is a factor market.

not.A: Goods and services = −40 − 70 = −$110bn; $225bn also includes net income.
not.C: The current account is in deficit by $140bn.
not.D: Capital transfers of +30 are a surplus on the capital account.

2010-4.why: At W1, above the equilibrium wage, more people want to work than firms want to employ. The gap is unemployment.

not.A: A higher wage reduces the quantity of labour demanded.
not.B: A higher wage attracts more people into the labour force.
not.D: The demand curve does not shift; firms move along it to a lower quantity.

2010-5.why: Removing protection forces uncompetitive manufacturers to close. Their workers' skills do not match the jobs available, raising structural unemployment.

not.A: Interest rates affect cyclical unemployment.
not.B: Government spending affects cyclical unemployment.
not.C: A change in how wages are set does not displace workers in the way that removing protection does.

2010-6.why: The IMF oversees the international monetary system and lends to countries in financial crisis.

not.A: The World Bank funds development.
not.B: The WTO oversees trade rules.
not.D: The OECD is a policy forum.

2010-7.why: Contribution = weight × price rise. Food 30 × 10 = 300; Health 10 × 30 = 300; Housing 15 × 25 = 375; Clothing 20 × 20 = 400. Clothing is the largest.

not.A: Food has the largest weight but the smallest price rise (300).
not.B: Health has the largest price rise but the smallest weight (300).
not.C: Housing contributes 375, less than Clothing.

2010-8.why: Lower labour costs and better infrastructure both reduce the cost of producing and moving Australian goods.

not.A: Higher interest rates raise firms' costs and push the dollar up.
not.C: Smaller import quotas are more protection, which reduces pressure to be efficient.
not.D: An appreciation makes exports dearer, offsetting the productivity gain.

2010-9.why: Cheap city parking encourages driving. Removing the tax concession makes driving in dearer, reducing congestion and pollution.

not.A: Cheaper petrol encourages more driving.
not.B: Free entry increases visitor numbers and damage to parks.
not.C: Smaller rebates discourage clean energy.

2010-10.why: From X to Y the economy is heading into a downturn. Buying securities lowers interest rates and an expansionary budget adds to demand.

not.B: Selling securities raises interest rates, working against the budget.
not.C: A contractionary budget would deepen the downturn.
not.D: Both would deepen the downturn.

2010-11.why: Less discretionary spending reduces demand. A depreciation makes imported goods and inputs dearer, raising costs.

not.A: Loose monetary policy adds to demand inflation.
not.B: More government spending adds to demand inflation.
not.C: More discretionary spending adds to demand inflation.

not.A: 0.2 does not come from these figures.
not.B: 0.5 is the MPC, not the multiplier.
not.C: A multiplier of 1 would mean nothing is re-spent.

2010-13.why: The government competes with firms for the same pool of savings, pushing interest rates up (crowding out).

not.A: Borrowing existing savings does not create money.

not.A: Lower subsidies raise producers' costs, shifting AS left.

not.D: Both shift the curves to the left.

2010-15.why: Public goods are non-rival: once provided, an extra user adds nothing to the cost.

not.B: No one can be excluded, so property rights are hard to define.

not.D: They are non-rival and non-excludable.

2010-17.why: Countries with a low HDI are less developed, and less developed countries typically have high birth rates.

not.A: Literacy is part of the HDI, so it is lower in Country A.

not.D: Institutions are weaker in less developed countries.

2010-18.why: Services have grown as finance and other services became globally integrated, and manufacturing has shrunk as tariffs were removed.

not.A: Stronger commodity demand would raise mining's share, not lower it.

not.D: Stronger demand for farm products would raise agriculture's share.

2010-20.why: A larger quota lets more imported cars in, so local producers hold a smaller share of the market.

not.A: More supply lowers the price.

not.D: A larger quota makes access easier.

not.A: Microeconomic reform is slow and is not mainly delivered through the Budget.

not.C: The terms of trade measure prices received, not how competitive firms are.
not.D: A higher dollar makes exports dearer.

2009-14.why: AS has shifted to the right. Deregulating labour markets makes labour more flexible and productive, lowering production costs.

2009-15.why: Interest on overseas borrowing is paid to foreigners, adding to the income deficit on the current account.

not.A: Borrowing overseas avoids pressure on domestic interest rates.
not.B: The money supply does not fall.

not.C: A higher MPC increases the multiplier.
not.D: Both are the wrong direction.

2009-17.why: Supply of Australian dollars has increased. Australians buying foreign assets must sell dollars to obtain foreign currency.

not.B: Fewer imports reduce the supply of dollars.
not.C: Foreigners' demand for Australian assets affects the demand for dollars.
not.D: Export demand affects the demand for dollars.

2009-18.why: Each 100 of extra income raises consumption by 50, so MPC = 0.5. Consumption rises by 100 (200 to 300), which needs income to rise by 200: Y = 600 + 200 = $800m.

not.A: $200m is the rise in income, not its new level.
not.B: $600m is the Year 3 level.
not.C: $700m adds only 100, which would mean an MPC of 1.

2009-19.why: People who do not look for work are not counted as unemployed or in the labour force, so the labour force shrinks by the jobs lost. The number unemployed is unchanged but is now a larger share of a smaller labour force.

not.A: The rate rises because the labour force is smaller.
not.C: The labour force shrinks because these people have left it.
not.D: The same number of unemployed in a smaller labour force is a higher rate.
